meta.status: DRAFT - written from general first-aid / public-health guidance. Must be reviewed and replaced with verified WHO / national guideline text by a qualified clinician before any real-world use.

scenarios.title: Dizziness
plain_descriptions: aankhon ke samne andhera aa raha hai
possible_contexts: low blood sugar (especially with diabetes medicines)
important_questions: Did you faint or almost faint?
Is the room spinning or do you feel like fainting?
Any chest pain, breathlessness or racing heartbeat?
Any face drooping, arm/leg weakness, trouble speaking or sudden vision loss?
Can you check BP and glucose?
Do you take BP or diabetes medicines?
red_flags: fainting, chest pain, breathlessness or racing/irregular heartbeat
face drooping, arm or leg weakness, speech difficulty, sudden vision loss or sudden severe headache
dizziness after a head injury
confusion
vomiting so much that fluids cannot be kept down
early_support: Sit or lie down straight away to avoid falling; stand up slowly afterwards.
Sip water or ORS if able to drink and not vomiting.
If you have not eaten for many hours, take a light snack.
Do not drive, climb or use machines while dizzy.
If BP/glucose can be measured, measure them and note the numbers.
escalation: Urgent care for any red flag.
See a healthcare professional within 24 hours if dizziness keeps returning, lasts more than a day, started after a new medicine, or the person is pregnant, elderly or has a chronic illness.
avoid: Do not assume low BP or 'low blood' without a measurement.
Do not advise starting, stopping or changing BP or diabetes medicines.
scenarios.referral_note: Nearest primary-care facility (BHU/RHC/clinic). BP, glucose and hemoglobin checks are commonly useful.
scenarios.source: General patient guidance aligned with NHS/WHO primary-care advice (draft)

scenarios.title: Weakness / Fatigue
important_questions: How long has this lasted?
Any fever, weight loss, or recent illness?
Any breathlessness, chest pain, or fainting?
Heavy periods or black stools?
Can you check BP, glucose and temperature?
red_flags: weakness on one side of the body or trouble speaking
chest pain, breathlessness at rest or fainting
confusion or extreme drowsiness
black stools or vomiting blood
extreme thirst with very frequent urination and vomiting
early_support: Rest and drink fluids regularly.
Eat regular balanced meals.
Check temperature, BP and glucose if you can and note the numbers.
Keep a short diary of when the weakness is worse.
escalation: Urgent care for any red flag.
See a healthcare professional if weakness lasts more than a few days, keeps returning or limits daily activity; testing may be needed.
avoid: Do not conclude a specific deficiency (blood, vitamin D, sugar) from symptoms alone.
Do not recommend high-dose supplements without testing.
scenarios.referral_note: Primary-care visit; CBC/hemoglobin, glucose and basic checks are commonly considered.
scenarios.source: General patient guidance aligned with NHS/WHO primary-care advice (draft)

scenarios.title: Fainting / Loss of consciousness
important_questions: Is the person awake and responding now?
Are they breathing normally?
Did they hurt their head or body when falling?
Any chest pain, palpitations or breathlessness before or after?
Any jerking movements or confusion after waking?
How long were they unconscious? Has this happened before?
Is she pregnant?
red_flags: still unconscious, hard to wake or confused
not breathing normally
chest pain, palpitations or breathlessness
seizure-like jerking
injury, especially to the head
fainted while exercising or while lying down
pregnancy
heavy bleeding
early_support: If the person has fainted and is breathing: lay them flat and, if there is no injury, raise the legs about 30 cm.
Loosen tight clothing and keep them in fresh air.
Once awake, keep them lying or sitting for 10-15 minutes and let them get up slowly.
Give small sips of water only when fully awake and able to swallow.
If unconscious but breathing, lay them on their side. Give nothing by mouth.
If not breathing normally, call emergency services and start CPR if you know how.
Check glucose if a meter is available.
escalation: Emergency care for any red flag.
Every fainting episode should be assessed by a healthcare professional, ideally the same day, especially a first episode.
avoid: Do not reassure that fainting is 'just weakness'.
Do not give food or drink to someone not fully awake.
scenarios.referral_note: Same-day primary-care or hospital assessment; BP lying/standing, glucose and ECG are commonly needed.
scenarios.source: General first-aid guidance aligned with Red Cross/NHS first-aid advice (draft)

scenarios.title: Blood sugar concerns (low or high)
plain_descriptions: mujhe diabetes hai aur ajeeb feel ho raha hai
symptom_patterns: extreme thirst, frequent urination, tiredness, blurred vision
possible_contexts: low glucose, especially with insulin or diabetes tablets, skipped meals or extra exercise
high glucose in known or undiagnosed diabetes
anxiety or other causes of shaking and sweating
important_questions: Has glucose actually been measured? What was the number?
Do you use insulin or diabetes tablets?
Are you fully awake, thinking clearly and able to swallow?
When did you last eat?
Any vomiting, stomach pain, fast breathing or extreme drowsiness?
red_flags: confusion, drowsiness, inability to swallow, seizure or unconsciousness
glucose below 54 mg/dL (3.0 mmol/L)
glucose that stays below 70 after two treatments
high glucose with vomiting, stomach pain, fast breathing, fruity breath or drowsiness
glucose of 400 mg/dL or more
early_support: Only if the person is awake, thinking clearly and able to swallow, and glucose is below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) OR low sugar is strongly suspected in someone using insulin/diabetes tablets: give about 15 g of fast sugar, such as 3-4 glucose tablets, half a glass (about 120 ml) of juice or regular soft drink, or about 1 tablespoon of sugar or honey in water.
Recheck glucose after 15 minutes; if still below 70 mg/dL repeat the same amount once, then eat a snack or meal.
Never give food or drink to someone who is drowsy, confused or cannot swallow; call emergency services.
For high readings without red flags: drink water, avoid sugary drinks, and contact a clinician the same day.
Write down the reading, the time, the last meal and medicines taken.
escalation: Emergency care for any red flag.
Anyone with repeated low or high readings, or first-time symptoms with a measured abnormal value, should see a clinician within 24 hours. Medicine changes must be made by a clinician.
avoid: Do not say 'you have low sugar' without a measurement; say it is possible.
Do not advise stopping or changing diabetes medicines or insulin doses.
Do not give anything by mouth to an unconscious or confused person.
scenarios.referral_note: Primary-care or diabetes clinic; HbA1c and review of medicines are commonly needed.
scenarios.source: Hypoglycemia '15-15 rule' and hyperglycemia warning signs as in general diabetes patient guidance (ADA/NHS-aligned, draft)

scenarios.title: Blood pressure concerns
plain_descriptions: بی پی ہائی لگ رہا ہے
symptom_patterns: headache, dizziness, flushing or no symptoms at all with high BP
dizziness, weakness, blurred vision with low BP
possible_contexts: stress, pain or recent activity raising a reading
dehydration or sudden standing lowering BP
measurement error from a wrongly sized cuff or rushed reading
important_questions: Was BP measured with a machine? What was the reading and time?
Any chest pain, breathlessness, severe headache, vision change, weakness or confusion?
Do you take BP medicines? Did you miss a dose?
Are you pregnant or recently delivered?
red_flags: BP 180/120 or higher WITH chest pain, breathlessness, weakness/numbness, speech or vision change, severe headache, confusion or seizure
very low BP with fainting or confusion
high BP or severe headache in pregnancy or after delivery
early_support: Sit quietly for 5 minutes with back supported, feet flat, arm resting at heart level, without talking, then measure; take a second reading after 1-2 minutes.
If 180/120 or higher without symptoms: rest, recheck in 5 minutes; if still that high, contact a healthcare professional the same day.
If BP is low with dizziness: sit or lie down, drink fluids, stand slowly.
Note readings with date and time to show the clinician.
escalation: Emergency care for any red flag.
Readings repeatedly at or above 140/90, or repeatedly below 90/60 with symptoms, need clinician review soon.
avoid: Do not decide high or low BP from symptoms alone.
Do not advise taking extra BP tablets or stopping prescribed ones.
scenarios.referral_note: Primary-care clinic for BP review; emergency department if red flags.
scenarios.source: General BP measurement and hypertensive-crisis guidance aligned with WHO/AHA patient advice (draft)

scenarios.title: Fever
possible_contexts: malaria or dengue where these occur
important_questions: What is the temperature and how long has it lasted?
How old is the patient? (babies under 3 months are higher risk)
Any stiff neck, rash, breathing difficulty, severe vomiting, bleeding or drowsiness?
Able to drink fluids and passing urine?
Any chronic illness or pregnancy?
red_flags: baby under 3 months with any fever
temperature of 40 °C (104 °F) or more
stiff neck, confusion, seizure, very drowsy
rash that does not fade when pressed
breathing difficulty
bleeding from nose or gums, severe stomach pain, black stools or persistent vomiting
cannot drink or very little urine
early_support: Rest and drink plenty of fluids (water, ORS).
Wear light clothing; use a lukewarm (not cold) sponge if uncomfortable.
If using an over-the-counter fever medicine, follow the label or pharmacist advice exactly, never combine products with the same ingredient, and do not give aspirin to children.
Measure temperature at the same time each day and note it.
escalation: Urgent care for any red flag.

See a healthcare professional if fever lasts more than 3 days, keeps returning, or the patient is a young child, elderly, pregnant or has a chronic illness. In dengue/malaria areas, prompt testing is advisable.
avoid: Do not give doses from memory; refer to the label or pharmacist.
Do not say the cause is dengue/malaria/typhoid without testing.
scenarios.referral_note: Primary-care visit; blood tests (e.g. CBC, malaria/dengue tests) may be needed.
scenarios.source: General fever self-care guidance aligned with WHO/NHS (draft)

scenarios.title: Dehydration / heat-related symptoms
symptom_patterns: thirst, dry mouth, dark urine, weakness, dizziness after heat or fluid loss
important_questions: Any vomiting, diarrhea or fever?
How much urine and what colour in the last 8 hours?
Can the person drink and keep fluids down?
Was there long heat exposure? What is the temperature?
Is the patient a child, elderly or diabetic?
red_flags: confusion, fainting or very drowsy
temperature of 40 °C or more with hot dry skin (possible heat stroke)
no urine for 8 hours or more
cannot keep fluids down
fast breathing or fast weak pulse
sunken eyes in a child
early_support: Move to shade or a cool place and rest.
Drink small, frequent sips of ORS prepared exactly as the packet says with clean water; plain water is also fine.
Loosen clothing and cool the skin with a wet cloth or fan.
Avoid very sugary drinks and heavy activity until recovered.
escalation: Emergency care for heat stroke or any red flag.
See a healthcare professional if not improving within a few hours of drinking fluids, or for children, elderly and diabetics with significant symptoms.
avoid: Do not give fluids to someone who is not fully awake.
Do not use ice-cold water baths on very weak patients without help.
scenarios.referral_note: Nearest facility for assessment and possible IV fluids if oral fluids fail.
scenarios.source: WHO ORS guidance and general heat-illness first aid (draft)

scenarios.title: Headache
symptom_patterns: head pain with or without nausea, light sensitivity or fever
important_questions: Did it start suddenly and is it the worst ever?
Any fever, stiff neck, vomiting, confusion, weakness, speech or vision change?
Any recent head injury?
Is BP available? Is the patient pregnant or recently delivered?
How long and how often?
red_flags: sudden, severe 'worst ever' headache
after head injury
with fever and stiff neck
with weakness, speech trouble, vision change, confusion or seizure
in pregnancy or after delivery, especially with high BP, swelling or vision change
new severe headache over age 50 or steadily worsening
early_support: Rest in a quiet, dim room and drink water.
Eat something if meals were missed.
Check BP if available and note it.
If using an over-the-counter pain medicine, follow the label or pharmacist advice.
escalation: Emergency care for any red flag.
See a healthcare professional if headaches are frequent, getting worse or not helped by simple measures.
avoid: Do not assume every headache is harmless.
Do not recommend medicine doses.
scenarios.referral_note: Primary-care visit; BP check and neurological assessment as needed.
scenarios.source: General headache red-flag guidance aligned with NHS/WHO (draft)

scenarios.title: Cough / breathing symptoms
important_questions: How long has the cough lasted?
Any difficulty breathing or inability to speak full sentences?
Fever, chest pain, coughing blood, wheeze?
Any known asthma, heart or lung disease? Is SpO2 available?
Age of the patient (small children and elderly are higher risk)?
red_flags: severe breathing difficulty or cannot speak full sentences
blue or grey lips
chest pain
coughing blood
SpO2 below 90%
fast breathing or chest in-drawing in a child
drowsiness or confusion
early_support: Sit upright, stay calm and loosen tight clothing.
Drink warm fluids; avoid smoke, dust and cooking smoke indoors.
Rest and keep the room ventilated.
Use a prescribed inhaler as your clinician instructed if you have asthma.
escalation: Emergency care for any red flag.
See a healthcare professional if cough lasts 2 weeks or more (TB testing may be needed), with fever for more than 3 days, or with wheeze.
avoid: Do not give cough medicines to small children without health-worker advice.
Do not downplay breathlessness.
scenarios.referral_note: Primary-care visit; chest examination, SpO2 and, if cough is 2 weeks or more, TB screening.
scenarios.source: General respiratory red-flag guidance aligned with WHO/NHS (draft)

scenarios.title: Vomiting / Diarrhea
symptom_patterns: repeated vomiting, watery stools, stomach cramps
important_questions: How many times in the last day, and for how long?
Able to drink and keep fluids down?
Blood in vomit or stool? Severe belly pain? Fever?
Age of the patient (infants, young children, elderly are higher risk)?
Passing urine normally?
red_flags: blood in vomit or stool, or black stool
severe or constant abdominal pain
signs of dehydration: very dry mouth, sunken eyes, no urine for 8 hours, drowsiness
cannot keep any fluids down
high fever
infant or very frail person with frequent watery stools
early_support: Give small, frequent sips of ORS prepared exactly as the packet says with clean water.
Continue eating light food when able; keep breastfeeding infants.
Wash hands with soap; use boiled or treated water.
For children with diarrhea, ask a health worker about zinc supplementation (dose is decided by the health worker).
escalation: Urgent care for red flags.
See a healthcare professional if it lasts more than 2 days in children or 3 days in adults, or sooner for infants, elderly and pregnant women.
avoid: Do not give anti-diarrhea medicines to children without advice.
Do not recommend antibiotics.
scenarios.referral_note: Nearest facility for rehydration and stool tests if needed.

scenarios.title: Minor burns / cuts
symptom_patterns: red painful skin, small blisters, small cuts
important_questions: Where is the burn and how big compared with the person's palm?
Is the skin white, charred or numb (deep burn)?
Chemical or electrical cause?
Is the patient a child, elderly or diabetic?
For cuts: is bleeding controlled? Tetanus vaccination status?
red_flags: burn larger than the person's palm, or on face, hands, feet, genitals or joints
chemical or electrical burn
deep, white, leathery or charred skin
smoke inhalation or breathing problems
burn in a young child or elderly person
bleeding that does not stop after 10 minutes of firm pressure
deep or gaping cut, or contaminated wound
early_support: Cool a burn under cool running water for 20 minutes as soon as possible.
Remove rings or tight items near the burn before swelling starts, unless stuck to skin.
Cover loosely with a clean non-fluffy dressing or cling film.
Do not apply toothpaste, butter, oil or ice; do not burst blisters.
For cuts: press firmly with a clean cloth for 10 minutes, then clean with clean water and cover.
escalation: Emergency or same-day care for any red flag.
See a healthcare professional if signs of infection appear (increasing pain, pus, spreading redness, fever).
avoid: No home remedies like toothpaste, butter, ink or oil.
Do not use ice directly on the skin.
scenarios.referral_note: Nearest clinic for dressing, tetanus review and wound assessment.
scenarios.source: General burn and wound first-aid guidance aligned with Red Cross/NHS (draft)

scenarios.title: Possible nutritional deficiency (vitamin D, iron/anemia)
plain_descriptions: vitamin D ki kami lagti hai
symptom_patterns: tiredness, body or muscle aches, pale skin, breathlessness on effort, hair loss, dizziness
important_questions: How long have symptoms lasted?
Any heavy periods, pregnancy, black stools or poor appetite?
Any breathlessness at rest, chest pain or fainting?
Have you had blood tests before?
red_flags: breathlessness at rest or chest pain
fainting
black stools or vomiting blood
heavy bleeding with dizziness
pregnancy with severe tiredness or paleness
early_support: Eat a balanced diet with iron-rich foods such as lentils, green leafy vegetables, meat or liver, along with vitamin C foods.
Get regular, sensible daytime sun exposure.
Keep a note of symptoms and take any previous reports to the clinician.
Do not start high-dose vitamin D or iron on your own; ask a clinician or pharmacist.
escalation: Urgent care for red flags.
Persistent symptoms should be assessed by a healthcare professional, who can decide whether blood tests (CBC/hemoglobin, ferritin, vitamin D) are appropriate.
avoid: Never say 'you have vitamin D deficiency/anemia' from symptoms alone; only a test can confirm.
Do not recommend supplement doses.
scenarios.referral_note: Primary-care visit; CBC/hemoglobin, ferritin and vitamin D testing as clinically appropriate.
scenarios.source: General nutrition and anemia patient guidance aligned with WHO/NHS (draft)
